questions.stem: What does 「おはようございます」 (ohayou gozaimasu) mean?
questions.explanation: 「おはようございます」 (ohayou gozaimasu) is the polite morning greeting. Between friends it shortens to 「おはよう」 (ohayou). Later in the day the greeting changes to 「こんにちは」 (konnichiwa).

questions.stem: What does 「こんばんは」 (konbanwa) mean?
questions.explanation: 「こんばんは」 (konbanwa) greets someone you meet in the evening. The final は is read wa, as in 「こんにちは」 (konnichiwa). 'Good night' is 「おやすみなさい」 (oyasuminasai), which is said when going to bed, not on meeting someone.

questions.stem: What does 「さようなら」 (sayounara) mean?
questions.explanation: 「さようなら」 (sayounara) is goodbye. It sounds rather final, so friends parting for the day usually say 「じゃあね」 (jaa ne) or 「またあした」 (mata ashita) instead.

questions.stem: What does 「おやすみなさい」 (oyasuminasai) mean?
questions.explanation: 「おやすみなさい」 (oyasuminasai) is said when someone is going to bed. It is not a greeting for meeting people at night: that is 「こんばんは」 (konbanwa), the most common mix-up.

questions.stem: What does 「ありがとうございます」 (arigatou gozaimasu) mean?
questions.explanation: 「ありがとうございます」 (arigatou gozaimasu) is the polite thank you; 「ありがとう」 (arigatou) alone is casual. 'You're welcome' is 「どういたしまして」 (dou itashimashite), a separate phrase.

questions.stem: What does 「すみません」 (sumimasen) mean?
questions.explanation: 「すみません」 (sumimasen) is excuse me, used to get attention, and it also works as a polite sorry. It is never a goodbye: that is 「さようなら」 (sayounara).

questions.stem: How do you say 'hello' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 「こんにちは」 (konnichiwa) is the everyday hello used during the day. 「こんばんは」 (konbanwa) is its evening partner, and both end in は read wa.

questions.stem: It is 8 am and you meet your teacher at the school gate. What do you say?
options: おはようございます (ohayou gozaimasu)
questions.explanation: Speaking to a teacher calls for the polite 「おはようございます」 (ohayou gozaimasu). The short 「おはよう」 (ohayou) is the right time of day but is only for friends and family, so a teacher would find it too casual.

questions.stem: At the start of a lesson the class leader calls 「きりつ」 (kiritsu). What does everyone do?
questions.explanation: 「きりつ」 (kiritsu) means stand up. The full routine is 「きりつ」 (stand), 「れい」 (rei, bow), then 「ちゃくせき」 (chakuseki, sit down).

questions.stem: After 「きりつ」 (kiritsu), the class leader calls 「れい」 (rei). What does the class do?
questions.explanation: 「れい」 (rei) is the call to bow to the teacher. It comes between 「きりつ」 (kiritsu, stand up) and 「ちゃくせき」 (chakuseki, sit down).

questions.stem: What does 「ちゃくせき」 (chakuseki) tell the class to do?
questions.explanation: 「ちゃくせき」 (chakuseki) means take your seats. It is the last call of the routine, after 「きりつ」 (kiritsu, stand up) and 「れい」 (rei, bow).

questions.stem: What does 「わかりません」 (wakarimasen) mean?
questions.explanation: 「わかりません」 (wakarimasen) is the negative of 「わかります」 (wakarimasu), so it means I don't understand. The ending ません (masen) makes a verb negative; 「わかりました」 (wakarimashita) means I understand.

questions.stem: You did not catch what the teacher said. How do you politely ask them to say it again?
options: もういちどおねがいします (mou ichido onegaishimasu)
ゆっくりおねがいします (yukkuri onegaishimasu)
ちょっとまってください (chotto matte kudasai)
よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu)
questions.explanation: 「もういちど」 (mou ichido) means one more time, and 「おねがいします」 (onegaishimasu) makes it a polite request. 「ゆっくり」 (yukkuri) asks for it slowly, which is a different request.

questions.stem: What does 「ゆっくりおねがいします」 (yukkuri onegaishimasu) mean?
questions.explanation: 「ゆっくり」 (yukkuri) means slowly. Asking for something to be said again is 「もういちどおねがいします」 (mou ichido onegaishimasu), the phrase it is most often confused with.

questions.stem: What does 「ちょっとまってください」 (chotto matte kudasai) mean?
questions.explanation: 「まって」 (matte) comes from まつ (matsu), to wait, and 「ちょっと」 (chotto) means a little. 〜てください (te kudasai) turns a verb into a polite request.

questions.stem: The teacher calls your name during the roll. What do you answer?
questions.explanation: 「はい」 (hai) means yes, and it is the reply to the roll, sometimes as 「はい、います」 (hai, imasu). 「いいえ」 (iie) is no, and 「どうぞ」 (douzo) is said when offering something.

questions.stem: A classmate hands you an eraser and says 「どうぞ」 (douzo). What do you reply?
questions.explanation: 「どうぞ」 (douzo) is said when offering something, so the reply is thanks: 「ありがとう」 (arigatou), or 「ありがとうございます」 to a teacher. Saying 「どうぞ」 back would be offering it to them again.

questions.stem: You arrive late to class. What do you say as you come in?
options: おくれてすみません (okurete sumimasen)
questions.explanation: 「おくれて」 (okurete) means being late, and 「すみません」 (sumimasen) apologises. 「いってきます」 (ittekimasu) is said when leaving home, and 「おつかれさま」 (otsukaresama) thanks people for their work.

questions.stem: How do you ask the teacher whether you may go to the toilet?
options: トイレに行ってもいいですか。 (toire ni itte mo ii desu ka.)
トイレに行きませんか。 (toire ni ikimasen ka.)
トイレに行ってください。 (toire ni itte kudasai.)
トイレはどこですか。 (toire wa doko desu ka.)
questions.explanation: 〜てもいいですか (te mo ii desu ka) asks permission: may I do it? 「行きませんか」 (ikimasen ka) is an invitation, 'won't you go?', and 「行ってください」 (itte kudasai) tells someone else to go.

questions.stem: You forgot your dictionary. How do you ask a friend to lend you theirs?
options: じしょをかしてください。 (jisho o kashite kudasai.)
じしょをかりてください。 (jisho o karite kudasai.)
じしょをかってください。 (jisho o katte kudasai.)
じしょをかえしてください。 (jisho o kaeshite kudasai.)
questions.explanation: かす (kasu) is to lend and かりる (kariru) is to borrow, so asking someone to lend uses 「かしてください」 (kashite kudasai). 「かりてください」 (karite kudasai) would ask them to borrow it, which is the classic mix-up.

questions.stem: What does 「はじめまして」 (hajimemashite) mean?
questions.explanation: 「はじめまして」 (hajimemashite) opens a self-introduction and is said only the very first time you meet someone. It literally means 'for the first time'.

questions.stem: You have just introduced yourself to the class. Which phrase normally ends a self-introduction?
options: よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu)
questions.explanation: A じこしょうかい (jikoshoukai, self-introduction) opens with 「はじめまして」 (hajimemashite) and closes with 「よろしくおねがいします」 (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), roughly 'I look forward to getting to know you'. Putting 「はじめまして」 at the end is the usual slip.

questions.stem: Someone asks you 「おなまえは？」 (onamae wa?). What are they asking?
questions.explanation: 「なまえ」 (namae) is name, and the お (o) in front makes it polite because it is the other person's. The question is left unfinished with は (wa), which is natural in casual speech.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I am Ken' in Japanese?
options: わたしをケンです。 (watashi o ken desu.)
わたしにケンです。 (watashi ni ken desu.)
わたしはケンます。 (watashi wa ken masu.)
わたしはケンです。 (watashi wa ken desu.)
questions.explanation: The pattern is A は B です (A wa B desu): A is B. The topic takes は, read wa. を (o) marks the object of an action verb and に (ni) a place or time, and ます (masu) ends verbs, never a name.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I am thirteen years old' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Age is counted with 〜さい (sai). 〜年 (nen) counts years in general, 〜人 (nin) counts people and 〜時 (ji) is o'clock, so the counter alone changes the meaning.

questions.stem: What does 「何さいですか。」 (nansai desu ka.) ask?
questions.explanation: 何 (nan) means what, and 〜さい (sai) counts years of age, so 「何さい」 (nansai) is how old. The year level question is 「何年生ですか。」 (nannensei desu ka.).

questions.stem: What does 「何年生ですか。」 (nannensei desu ka.) ask?
options: What year level are you in?
questions.explanation: 〜年生 (nensei) is a student's year level, so 「何年生」 (nannensei) asks which year you are in. Age is asked with 「何さい」 (nansai) instead.

questions.stem: What does 「八年生です。」 (hachinensei desu.) mean?
questions.explanation: 〜年生 (nensei) gives the year level, so 「八年生」 (hachinensei) is Year 8, the way Australian students describe themselves. Eight years old would be 「八さい」 (hassai).

questions.stem: When do you add 「〜さん」 (san) to a name?
questions.explanation: 〜さん (san) follows another person's name to show respect, and it is never added to your own. Teachers take 〜先生 (sensei) instead, also placed after the name.

questions.stem: How do you address your teacher, Ms Tanaka, in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 先生 (sensei) is a title that goes after the name, the reverse of English 'Ms Tanaka'. 〜くん (kun) and 〜ちゃん (chan) are for friends and children, so they would be far too familiar for a teacher.

questions.stem: How do you say 'four' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Four is 「よん」 (yon), and it also has the reading し (shi). Many counting words prefer よん because し sounds like the word for death.

questions.stem: What does 「なな」 (nana) mean?
questions.explanation: 「なな」 (nana) is seven; its other reading is しち (shichi). Four is よん (yon) and nine is きゅう (kyuu).

questions.stem: How do you say '15' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Japanese builds numbers like a sum: ten then five, じゅう + ご (juu + go). Putting the five first, 「ごじゅう」 (gojuu), means five tens, which is 50.

questions.stem: What number is 「よんじゅうはち」 (yonjuuhachi)?
questions.explanation: よん (yon) before じゅう (juu) means four tens, and はち (hachi) after it adds eight: 40 + 8. 84 would be はちじゅうよん (hachijuuyon), with the parts swapped.

questions.stem: What does 「ひゃく」 (hyaku) mean?
questions.explanation: 「ひゃく」 (hyaku) is 100, written 百. One thousand is せん (sen), 千, and ten thousand is いちまん (ichiman).

questions.stem: How do you say '300' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: After さん (san), ひゃく changes its sound to びゃく (byaku). The p sound belongs to 600 and 800, ろっぴゃく (roppyaku) and はっぴゃく (happyaku), and 「さんぜん」 (sanzen) is 3,000.

questions.stem: How do you say '600' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: ろく + ひゃく contracts to 「ろっぴゃく」 (roppyaku), with a small っ and a p sound. The same happens in はっぴゃく (happyaku), 800. 「ろくせん」 (rokusen) is 6,000.

questions.stem: What number is 「さんぜんごひゃく」 (sanzengohyaku)?
questions.explanation: さんぜん (sanzen) is 3,000 and ごひゃく (gohyaku) is 500, so together they make 3,500. 3,050 would be さんぜんごじゅう (sanzengojuu).

questions.stem: What does 「千円」 (sen'en) mean?
questions.explanation: 千 (sen) is a thousand and 円 (en) is yen, the Japanese currency. The apostrophe in sen'en shows that ん and え are separate sounds.

questions.stem: How do you say '20 years old' in Japanese, using its special word?
questions.explanation: Twenty years old has its own word, 「はたち」 (hatachi). 「はつか」 (hatsuka) is the 20th of the month and 「にじゅうにん」 (nijuunin) is twenty people.

questions.stem: How do you say 'two people' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: One and two people have special readings: ひとり (hitori) and 「ふたり」 (futari). From three it is regular, さんにん (sannin). 「ふたつ」 (futatsu) counts two things, not people.

questions.stem: In a phone number, how is the dash between groups of digits usually read aloud?
questions.explanation: A dash in a phone number is read の (no), so 03-1234 is ぜろさんの、いちにさんよん (zero san no, ichi ni san yon). と (to) means and, which would join the groups as a list.

questions.stem: Someone asks 「でんわばんごうは何ばんですか。」 (denwa bangou wa nanban desu ka.) What do they want?
questions.explanation: 「でんわ」 (denwa) is telephone and 「ばんごう」 (bangou) is number. 「何ばん」 (nanban) asks which number.

questions.stem: How do you say 'four o'clock' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Four o'clock is 「よじ」 (yoji), using the short reading よ (yo) that 四 also has in 四人 (yonin). Neither よんじ nor しじ is said. 「よじかん」 (yojikan) is four hours, a length of time rather than a time of day.

questions.stem: How do you say 'nine o'clock' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Nine o'clock uses the reading く (ku): 「くじ」 (kuji). 「きゅうじ」 is the natural guess from きゅう (kyuu), but it is not used for the time. 「くじはん」 (kujihan) is half past nine.

questions.stem: What does 「三時半」 (sanjihan) mean?
questions.explanation: 半 (han) means half, and after 〜時 (ji) it means half past. Three hours would be 三じかん (sanjikan).

questions.stem: What time is 「六時十分」 (rokuji juppun)?
questions.explanation: The hour comes first, then the minutes: 六時 (rokuji) is six o'clock and 十分 (juppun) is ten minutes. 6:30 would be 六時半 (rokujihan).

questions.stem: What time is 「十時四十五分」 (juuji yonjuugofun)?
questions.explanation: 十時 (juuji) is ten o'clock and 四十五分 (yonjuugofun) is 45 minutes. Japanese says the hour first and then the minutes, so there is nothing like 'quarter to eleven' to convert.

questions.stem: Which of these says 8:05 in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Japanese gives the hour before the minutes, so 8:05 is 八時五分 (hachiji gofun). Following the English 'five past eight' puts the minutes first, which Japanese does not do.

questions.stem: How do you read 「一分」, one minute?
questions.explanation: いち + ふん contracts to 「いっぷん」 (ippun): a small っ and a p sound. The p sound also appears in さんぷん (sanpun) and ろっぷん (roppun), while ごふん (gofun) keeps the f.

questions.stem: How do you ask 'What time is it now?' in Japanese?
options: 今、何さいですか。 (ima, nansai desu ka.)
今、何時ですか。 (ima, nanji desu ka.)
今、何じかんですか。 (ima, nanjikan desu ka.)
今、何日ですか。 (ima, nannichi desu ka.)
questions.explanation: 何時 (nanji) asks what o'clock. 何じかん (nanjikan) asks how many hours, 何日 (nannichi) asks the date and 何さい (nansai) asks age.

questions.stem: What does 「月よう日」 (getsuyoubi) mean?
questions.explanation: 月 (getsu) is the moon, so 「月よう日」 (getsuyoubi) is moon day, Monday, as in English. Sunday is 日よう日 (nichiyoubi), sun day.

questions.stem: What does 「火よう日」 (kayoubi) mean?
questions.explanation: 火 (ka) is fire, and 「火よう日」 (kayoubi) is Tuesday. The weekdays follow the elements in order: fire, water, wood, metal, earth.

questions.stem: What does 「金よう日」 (kin'youbi) mean?
questions.explanation: 金 (kin) is gold or metal, and 「金よう日」 (kin'youbi) is Friday. Saturday is 土よう日 (doyoubi), earth day.

questions.stem: What does 「日よう日」 (nichiyoubi) mean?
questions.explanation: 日 (nichi) is the sun, so 「日よう日」 (nichiyoubi) is sun day, Sunday. The second 日 in the word is read び (bi).

questions.stem: How do you say 'Wednesday' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 水 (sui) is water, and 「水よう日」 (suiyoubi) is Wednesday. 火よう日 (kayoubi), fire day, comes just before it on Tuesday.

questions.stem: How do you say 'Saturday' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 土 (do) is earth or soil, and 「土よう日」 (doyoubi) is Saturday. Sunday, 日よう日 (nichiyoubi), is the usual mix-up because the weekend days are learned together.

questions.stem: What does 「あした」 (ashita) mean?
questions.explanation: 「あした」 (ashita) is tomorrow. Today is きょう (kyou) and yesterday is きのう (kinou).

questions.stem: How do you say 'today' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Today is 「きょう」 (kyou), with a blended きょ sound. 「きのう」 (kinou) is yesterday; the two look and sound close, so read the small ょ carefully.

questions.stem: You are telling your teacher about your own mother. Which word do you use?
questions.explanation: Talking about your own family to someone outside it, Japanese uses the plain word: 「はは」 (haha), written 母. 「おかあさん」 (okaasan) is for someone else's mother, or for calling your own mother directly.

questions.stem: You ask a friend about their father. Which word do you use?
questions.explanation: Someone else's father is 「おとうさん」 (otousan), written お父さん. 「ちち」 (chichi) is only for your own father. 「おじさん」 (ojisan) is uncle and 「おじいさん」 (ojiisan) is grandfather.

questions.stem: What does 「あに」 (ani) mean?
questions.explanation: 「あに」 (ani) is your own older brother. Someone else's older brother is おにいさん (oniisan), and your younger brother is おとうと (otouto).

questions.stem: What does 「いもうと」 (imouto) mean?
questions.explanation: 「いもうと」 (imouto) is younger sister. Younger brother is おとうと (otouto); the two end in the same sound, which is where the confusion comes from.

questions.stem: How do you say 'younger brother' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Younger brother is 「おとうと」 (otouto). 「おとうさん」 (otousan) begins with the same sounds but means father, so listen for the ending.

questions.stem: Which word means someone else's older sister?
questions.explanation: 「おねえさん」 (oneesan) is someone else's older sister, with a long ええ. 「あね」 (ane) means older sister too, but only your own.

questions.stem: How do you say 'family' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 「かぞく」 (kazoku) is family. 「りょうしん」 (ryoushin) is parents, and 「友だち」 (tomodachi) is friend.

questions.stem: A friend says 「かぞくは四人です。」 (kazoku wa yonin desu.) What does this tell you?
options: There are four people in the family.
questions.explanation: 〜人 (nin) counts people, and four people is 四人 (yonin). The sentence counts everyone in the family, including the speaker.

questions.stem: A friend says 「あには十七さいです。」 (ani wa juunanasai desu.) What do you learn?
options: Their older brother is in Year 7.
questions.explanation: 「あに」 (ani) is the speaker's own older brother, and 〜さい (sai) gives age, so he is seventeen. Year 7 would use 〜年生 (nensei).

questions.stem: Your teacher asks 「お母さんは何さいですか。」 (okaasan wa nansai desu ka.) Your mother is 45. Which is the best answer?
options: 母は五十四さいです。 (haha wa gojuuyonsai desu.)
母は四十五年です。 (haha wa yonjuugonen desu.)
母を四十五さいです。 (haha o yonjuugosai desu.)
母は四十五さいです。 (haha wa yonjuugosai desu.)
questions.explanation: The teacher says お母さん (okaasan) because it is your mother, not theirs; you answer with 母 (haha). 四十五 (yonjuugo) is 45, age takes 〜さい (sai), and the topic takes は (wa).

questions.stem: What does 「すうがく」 (suugaku) mean?
questions.explanation: 「すうがく」 (suugaku) is maths, from すう (suu), number. Science is かがく (kagaku) and music is おんがく (ongaku): many subjects end in がく (gaku), meaning study.

questions.stem: What does 「たいいく」 (taiiku) mean?
questions.explanation: 「たいいく」 (taiiku) is physical education. Art is びじゅつ (bijutsu) and music is おんがく (ongaku).

questions.stem: How do you say 'science' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Science is 「かがく」 (kagaku). 「すうがく」 (suugaku) is maths and 「おんがく」 (ongaku) is music; all three end in がく (gaku), so the first syllable decides.

questions.stem: How do you say 'English' (the subject) in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 〜ご (go) means language, so English is 「えいご」 (eigo). 「えいが」 (eiga) differs by one sound and means a film.

questions.stem: What does 「おんがく」 (ongaku) mean?
questions.explanation: 「おんがく」 (ongaku) is music, from おん (on), sound. It is easily mixed up with すうがく (suugaku), maths, because of the shared がく (gaku).

questions.stem: What does 「れきし」 (rekishi) mean?
questions.explanation: 「れきし」 (rekishi) is history. Geography is ちり (chiri) and science is かがく (kagaku).

questions.stem: What does 「しゅみ」 (shumi) mean?
questions.explanation: 「しゅみ」 (shumi) is a hobby or interest. 「しゅみは何ですか。」 (shumi wa nan desu ka.) asks what someone's hobby is.

questions.stem: A friend says 「しゅみはどくしょです。」 (shumi wa dokusho desu.) What is their hobby?
questions.explanation: 「どくしょ」 (dokusho) is reading, especially books for pleasure. Cooking would be りょうり (ryouri).

questions.stem: What does 「えいが」 (eiga) mean?
questions.explanation: 「えいが」 (eiga) is a film or movie. It is one sound away from えいご (eigo), English, and えき (eki) is a station.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I like music' in Japanese?
options: おんがくがすきです。 (ongaku ga suki desu.)
おんがくをすきです。 (ongaku o suki desu.)
おんがくにすきです。 (ongaku ni suki desu.)
おんがくですきです。 (ongaku de suki desu.)
questions.explanation: The thing you like is marked with が (ga): 〜がすきです (ga suki desu). English 'I like music' makes music an object, which tempts learners into を (o), but すき (suki) is an adjective, not a verb.

questions.stem: What does 「サッカーがだいすきです。」 (sakkaa ga daisuki desu.) mean?
questions.explanation: だい (dai) means big, so 「だいすき」 (daisuki) is a strong like: love. Being good at something is 〜がじょうずです (ga jouzu desu).

questions.stem: What does 「しゅくだいがきらいです。」 (shukudai ga kirai desu.) mean?
questions.explanation: 「きらい」 (kirai) is the opposite of すき (suki): dislike. Like すき, it takes が (ga) for the thing disliked.

questions.stem: Someone asks 「スポーツがすきですか。」 (supootsu ga suki desu ka.) You do like sport. How do you answer?
options: いいえ、すきです。 (iie, suki desu.)
はい、すきじゃないです。 (hai, suki ja nai desu.)
はい、すきです。 (hai, suki desu.)
questions.explanation: Yes is はい (hai), and the answer repeats すきです (suki desu). すき (suki) is an adjective, so it never takes the verb ending ます (masu), and いいえ (iie) with a positive answer contradicts itself.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I don't like tomatoes very much' in Japanese?
options: トマトはあまりすきじゃないです。 (tomato wa amari suki ja nai desu.)
トマトはあまりすきです。 (tomato wa amari suki desu.)
トマトはとてもすきじゃないです。 (tomato wa totemo suki ja nai desu.)
トマトはあまりきらいです。 (tomato wa amari kirai desu.)
questions.explanation: 「あまり」 (amari), not very much, is always followed by a negative, so it pairs with すきじゃないです (suki ja nai desu). 「とても」 (totemo), very, does not pair with すきじゃない, and きらいです (kirai desu) has no negative ending for あまり to go with.

questions.stem: Someone asks 「何がすきですか。」 (nani ga suki desu ka.) What do they want to know?
questions.explanation: 何 (nani) is what, and 〜がすきですか (ga suki desu ka) asks about liking. Before が (ga), 何 is read なに (nani) rather than なん (nan).

questions.stem: What does 「あさごはん」 (asagohan) mean?
questions.explanation: あさ (asa) is morning and ごはん (gohan) is a meal or cooked rice, so 「あさごはん」 (asagohan) is breakfast. Lunch is ひるごはん (hirugohan).

questions.stem: How do you say 'lunch' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: ひる (hiru) is midday, so lunch is 「ひるごはん」 (hirugohan). 「ばんごはん」 (bangohan) is dinner, from ばん (ban), evening.

questions.stem: What do people say just before they start eating a meal?
options: ごちそうさまでした (gochisousama deshita)
questions.explanation: 「いただきます」 (itadakimasu) is said before eating, expressing thanks for the food. 「ごちそうさまでした」 (gochisousama deshita) is its partner, said after the meal.

questions.stem: What does 「おいしい」 (oishii) mean?
questions.explanation: 「おいしい」 (oishii) is delicious or tasty. Sweet is あまい (amai) and spicy is からい (karai).

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'I eat sushi'?
options: すしを見ます。 (sushi o mimasu.)
すしを食べます。 (sushi o tabemasu.)
すしを飲みます。 (sushi o nomimasu.)
すしに食べます。 (sushi ni tabemasu.)
questions.explanation: 食べます (tabemasu) is eat, and を (o) marks what is eaten. 飲みます (nomimasu) is drink and 見ます (mimasu) is see, while に (ni) marks a time or place rather than an object.

questions.stem: What does 「はれ」 (hare) mean, said about the weather?
questions.explanation: 「はれ」 (hare) is fine, sunny weather. Cloudy is くもり (kumori), rain is あめ (ame) and snow is ゆき (yuki).

questions.stem: The weather forecast says 「あしたはあめです。」 (ashita wa ame desu.) What will the weather be tomorrow?
questions.explanation: In a forecast, 「あめ」 (ame) is rain. The same kana also spell a word for a sweet, which is why context matters with this word.

questions.stem: How do you say 'It is cold' about the weather?
questions.explanation: 「さむい」 (samui) is cold weather. 「つめたい」 (tsumetai) is cold to the touch, like a drink, and 「すずしい」 (suzushii) is pleasantly cool.

questions.stem: Said about the weather, what does 「あついです。」 (atsui desu.) mean?
questions.explanation: 「あつい」 (atsui) is hot. Warm is あたたかい (atatakai), a gentler word, and cold is さむい (samui).

questions.stem: How do you say 'It is not cold today' in Japanese?
options: きょうはさむいないです。 (kyou wa samui nai desu.)
きょうはさむくです。 (kyou wa samuku desu.)
きょうはさむくないです。 (kyou wa samukunai desu.)
きょうはさむいじゃないです。 (kyou wa samui ja nai desu.)
questions.explanation: An い-adjective makes its negative by changing the final い to くない (kunai): さむい becomes さむくない. じゃない (ja nai) belongs to nouns and な-adjectives, so adding it to さむい is the most common error.

questions.stem: How do you say 'small' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Small is 「小さい」 (chiisai). Its opposite is 「大きい」 (ookii), and both end in the い of an い-adjective.

questions.stem: What does 「おもしろい」 (omoshiroi) mean?
questions.explanation: 「おもしろい」 (omoshiroi) is interesting, and it can also mean funny. Boring is つまらない (tsumaranai).

questions.stem: What does 「むずかしい」 (muzukashii) mean?
questions.explanation: 「むずかしい」 (muzukashii) is difficult. Easy is やさしい (yasashii) and busy is いそがしい (isogashii).

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'Japanese is fun'?
options: 日本ごはたのしいです。 (nihongo wa tanoshii desu.)
日本ごはたのしいなです。 (nihongo wa tanoshii na desu.)
日本ごをたのしいです。 (nihongo o tanoshii desu.)
日本ごはたのしです。 (nihongo wa tanoshi desu.)
questions.explanation: 「たのしい」 (tanoshii) is an い-adjective, so です (desu) follows it directly with nothing between. な (na) is used only with な-adjectives before a noun, and the final い is part of the word.
